title: How good is student-to-student listening in your school? 76f954ea1613174bfd109f4352c786b2c32d6560378c2c084a1b5a74
author: Oracy Cambridge
summary: This opening installment of a six-part Oracy Cambridge series on implementing oracy, written by Topsy on behalf of the team, argues that listening is the neglected half of speaking and listening and that school leaders should examine how well students listen to one another rather than to the teacher. It proposes three observable indicators for walkthroughs of pair, group and whole-class talk. The first is the content of responses: whether a student connects to, builds on, questions or challenges what a peer has said, with sentence stems such as going back to what Cleo said. The second is body language and action, including note taking while peers speak, which the piece treats as an active listening strategy. The third and most important is whether one student's contribution changes what the next student says. The piece closes by reframing the observer's question from whether students are listening to what evidence shows they have listened to each other. It is a brief, practical diagnostic that ends with a promotional note for the Implementing Oracy 2027 programme.
points: The piece claims students often listen reasonably well to teachers but far less well to each other, which is where observation should focus.
Verbal clues of real listening include explicit references back to a named classmate's point, requests for clarification, and deliberate challenges.
Students writing while peers talk, by jotting key words or mind-mapping the discussion, is treated as visible evidence of active listening.
The strongest test is whether talk is cumulative: if students merely take turns giving their own answers, there is plenty of talk but little listening.
quotes: When you look at oracy practices in your school, it is worth taking time to look at the quality of student-to-student listening. Often, students listen fairly well to teachers, but not always to each other.
Are students genuinely listening to what each other has to say, or are they simply waiting for their turn to speak?
Look at their responses. Do they connect to what someone else has said? Do they agree or disagree with it? Do they ask a question because they want to understand what another student means?
Making notes, especially of key words and phrases is a great active listening strategy.
A student might change their mind, add something to an idea, make a connection or challenge a point because of what they have heard.
If they are simply taking turns to give their own answers, there may be plenty of talk but not much listening.
